analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and replaces it with high-risk pool funding, interstate insurance sales, and association health plans.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to eight House committees, sent to one subcommittee, and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the Affordable Care Act and the companion 2010 health law in full, wiping out their coverage expansions and consumer protections as if they had never passed. In their place it would fund state high-risk pools for sick people at $5 billion a year, let insurers sell individual policies across state lines under the rules of whichever state the insurer picks, let trade and professional associations sponsor group health plans exempt from most state insurance rules, and remove the income floor on the tax deduction for medical expenses. It was introduced in the final months of a Congress whose House majority had just passed the health law, and it never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurers would gain the most: they could choose a primary state and sell policies into every other state without that state's benefit mandates, rate rules, or consumer protections, and they could sell skimpier plans to healthy buyers. Trade associations, chambers of commerce, and small employers could pool workers into association health plans outside state insurance regulation. Higher-income taxpayers with large medical bills would gain from the unlimited deduction. People who are healthy and don't use much care could buy cheaper, thinner policies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insurers, trade associations, and higher-income itemizers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 as if they had never been enacted, restoring the law that existed before [S2][S3].
Removes the 7.5%-of-income floor on the medical expense deduction, so every dollar of medical costs could be deducted by itemizers [S2][S3].
Authorizes $5 billion per year for fiscal 2011 through 2015 in grants to states to create and run high-risk pools for people insurers will not cover [S2][S3].

Lets an insurer designate one 'primary state' and sell individual coverage into every other state, exempt from the secondary state's insurance laws except a short list covering solvency, taxes, fraud, and claims-settlement abuses [S2][S3].

Creates certified association health plans under ERISA — group plans sponsored by bona fide trade, professional, and business associations — largely outside state insurance regulation, with a federal fund to pay insurers if a plan collapses [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: People with preexisting conditions and expensive medical needs would bear the cost: the bill repeals the health law's protections and guarantees and offers high-risk pools instead, which historically enrolled few people at high premiums. States would lose their power to set benefit mandates and rate rules for coverage sold into their markets. The Treasury would lose revenue from the expanded medical deduction, borne by all taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with preexisting conditions, states, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Full repeal would have stripped the health law's protections and benefits — including its coverage expansions and rules barring insurers from turning away or pricing out sick customers — restoring the pre-2010 insurance market [S2][S3].

Interstate sales let an insurer pick the lightest-regulated state and export its rules nationwide, weakening the benefit mandates and consumer protections of every other state; the bill's own required disclosure tells buyers the policy 'is not subject to all of the consumer protection laws or restrictions on rate changes' of their home state [S3].

The unlimited medical deduction is worth the most to taxpayers with the largest medical bills relative to income — higher earners who itemize — and its cost to the Treasury is carried by all taxpayers [S2].

High-risk pools are a narrower substitute than the health law's universal protections: pools serve only the people who cannot buy coverage at all, and they historically charged high premiums, so the bill spends $5 billion a year without guaranteeing affordable coverage for sick people [S2][S3].

Association health plans exempted from state rules have historically been prone to insolvency and fraud; this bill responds with solvency requirements and a federal rescue fund, but still leaves plan sponsors as the ones running their members' coverage outside state oversight [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver real savings and flexibility to a specific group — insurers, associations, and healthy, higher-income buyers — while dismantling the health law's framework for covering sick and lower-income people and replacing it with thinner programs (high-risk pools, cross-border plans) that shift risk back onto the people least able to bear it. Even the bill's own cross-border provisions acknowledge buyers would lose benefit mandates, rate protections, and consumer laws. The design concentrates its advantages with concentrated interests.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2010, referred to eight committees and then one subcommittee, and no committee ever acted on it before the Congress expired in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Broun, a Georgia Republican, introduced the bill on May 27, 2010, with Rep. John Shadegg as the other original sponsor [S1][S3][S5].

The same day, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee plus seven others — Appropriations, Ways and Means, Education and Labor, Judiciary, Natural Resources, Rules, and House Administration — with the Speaker to decide which committee would take the lead [S5].
On June 29, 2010 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, and that was the last action recorded [S5].
Only 3 of the House's 178 Republicans cosponsored the bill [S4].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 with the bill dead [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The health law and the people who had just won its protections came out ahead: the repeal never advanced, and the Affordable Care Act remained on the books. No industry gained, since nothing changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The health law and its beneficiaries

for.name: Rep. John Shadegg
for.what_they_did: Joined Broun as the second original sponsor at introduction

against.name: Rep. Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in committee under the referral rule and never brought it to the floor in a chamber her party controlled 253 to 178

against.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing in the primary committee, leaving the bill to die at the subcommittee stage

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican (3 of 178 House Republicans), and the Democratic House majority that had just passed the health law took no action on the repeal.

industries.note: Full repeal would remove the health law's requirements and its customer expansions, while the cross-border and association plan provisions would free insurers to sell cheaper, skimpier policies to healthy buyers under the friendliest state's rules. The gain comes from weaker coverage protections for the people who need insurance most.

industries.industry: Trade associations, chambers of commerce, and plan sponsors
industries.note: The bill creates certified association health plans that let associations pool small employers into group coverage largely outside state insurance regulation. It includes solvency rules, trustee requirements, and a federal rescue fund, but leaves sponsors running members' coverage outside state oversight.

Self-insured association plans would be required to buy excess/stop-loss and indemnification insurance from insurers, and the federal fund would pay designated insurers to keep coverage in force if a plan fails — a guaranteed revenue stream built into the bill.

industries.industry: Higher-income taxpayers with large medical expenses
industries.note: Removing the 7.5%-of-income floor makes the medical deduction unlimited, which is worth most to itemizers with big medical bills relative to income. The lost revenue is carried by all taxpayers.

Interstate sales would exempt insurers from a secondary state's benefit mandates, rating rules, and consumer protections, and association plans would be preempted from most state regulation, shrinking the states' authority over coverage sold to their own residents. States would keep narrow powers over solvency, fraud, and claims-settlement abuse.
